entries.title: COIN TYPE
COLLABORATIVE TRANSACTION
entries.body: Bitcoin transaction that involves several different entities as inputs of the transaction. It is therefore also a transaction model that can be used in chain analysis. The typical example of a collaborative transaction is the coinjoin, where several users pool their UTXOs as inputs to recover the sum (minus transaction fees) in outputs of the same amount, in order to prevent tracing by breaking the history of the coins.

entries.title: COMMITMENT TRANSACTION
entries.body: In the context of a bidirectional channel within Lightning, the commitment transaction is a transaction that both parties create and sign, without however publishing it on the main chain. It represents the current state of the distribution of funds between the parties of a channel, each Lightning payment resulting in a new commitment transaction. These transactions are valid, but are only broadcast when the channel is closed unilaterally. They contain outputs for each party, reflecting the distribution of funds according to the Lightning payments made since the channel was opened. Penalty mechanisms are associated to deter the parties from broadcasting obsolete states of the channel, that is, old commitment transactions that reflect an incorrect distribution of funds.

entries.title: FUNDING TRANSACTION
entries.body:
On-chain Bitcoin transaction that marks the opening of a payment channel on the Lightning Network. It sends funds to a 2/2 multisignature address jointly controlled by the two parties of the channel. These funds make up the total capacity of the channel and can only be spent if both participants sign together.

Before publishing the funding transaction on the blockchain, the channel initiator first builds a commitment transaction (*commitment transaction*) signed by both parties. This precaution guarantees that the initiator will be able to recover their funds even if their peer becomes uncooperative. The channel is considered open once the funding transaction is confirmed. Its output identifier (`txid:output_index`) constitutes the *channel point*, which serves as a unique reference to identify the channel throughout its lifetime.

entries.title: NOTIFICATION TRANSACTION
entries.body:
Specific Bitcoin transaction used within the BIP-0047 protocol (reusable payment codes). The notification transaction is the first step required to establish a payment link between two users via their respective payment codes.

Concretely, when Alice wants to send payments to Bob using his payment code, she must first send him a notification transaction. This transaction contains, in an `OP_RETURN` output, Alice's payment code encrypted using a shared secret computed with ECDH (*Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman*). Bob, by monitoring his notification address, can decrypt this information and discover Alice's payment code. He can then derive the corresponding addresses to identify Alice's future payments.

The notification transaction only needs to be sent once for each pair of users. Subsequent payments between Alice and Bob no longer require this step.

entries.title: PENALTY TRANSACTION
entries.body:
Bitcoin transaction used on the Lightning Network to punish a peer who has published an old, revoked commitment transaction on the blockchain. It allows the wronged party to recover all of the channel's funds, including the attacker's share.

The mechanism relies on revocation keys. When a channel state is updated, each party gives the other a key that makes it possible to spend all of the funds if the old state were to be published. If a node tries to cheat by broadcasting an old commitment, its peer has a time window in which to detect the fraud and build the penalty transaction using this revocation key. This time window is guaranteed by a timelock `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` on the cheater's output.

*Watchtowers* are third-party services that monitor the blockchain continuously to detect such frauds and broadcast penalty transactions on behalf of offline nodes.

entries.title: STANDARD TRANSACTION
entries.body:
Bitcoin transaction that, in addition to complying with the consensus rules, also falls within the standardization rules configured by default on Bitcoin Core nodes. These standardization rules are enforced individually by each Bitcoin node, in addition to the consensus rules, to define the structure of the unconfirmed transactions it accepts into its mempool and broadcasts to its peers.

These rules are therefore configured and executed locally by each node and can vary from one node to another. They apply exclusively to unconfirmed transactions. Thus, a node will only accept a transaction it would judge non-standard if that transaction is already included in a valid block. 

Note that the majority of nodes leave the default configurations as pre-established in Bitcoin Core, which in effect creates a homogeneity of standardization rules across the network. A transaction that, although compliant with the consensus rules, does not comply with these standardization rules will have difficulty propagating on the network. It can nevertheless be included in a valid block if it ever reaches a miner. In practice, these transactions, described as non-standard, are often transmitted directly to a miner through channels external to Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network. This is often the only way to confirm this type of transaction. For example, a transaction that allocates no fees is both valid under the consensus rules and non-standard, because Bitcoin Core's default policy for the `minRelayTxFee` parameter is `0.000001` (in BTC/kvB).

entries.title: TAIL EMISSION
entries.body:
A monetary policy mechanism that consists of maintaining a fixed block reward indefinitely after the initial issuance schedule of a cryptocurrency has been exhausted. Unlike Bitcoin's model, where the block subsidy gradually decreases through *halvings* until it reaches zero, a *tail emission* guarantees a constant flow of newly created units with each block. Although highly controversial, it is a proposal that occasionally resurfaces in debates around Bitcoin.

Monero is the most notable example of this approach: since June 2022, each block has produced a fixed reward of 0.6 XMR, after the main issuance of approximately 18.1 million units was exhausted.

Supporters of *tail emission* argue that it solves the problem of funding network security in the long term by guaranteeing a permanent incentive for miners, without depending exclusively on transaction fees. They also maintain that the inevitable loss of coins (forgotten keys, deaths of holders) would naturally offset the monetary creation, causing the circulating supply to converge toward a stable equilibrium. Opponents consider that it contradicts the principle of a fixed and deterministic maximum supply, a fundamental characteristic of Bitcoin. They also argue that permanent inflation dilutes the value of existing units and that a sufficiently developed transaction fee market can secure the network on its own in the long term.

In the context of Bitcoin, adding a *tail emission* would require a *hard fork* and is a highly controversial proposal. Bitcoin's fixed monetary policy, with a cap of 21 million bitcoins, is considered by a large part of the community to be a fundamental attribute of the protocol.

entries.title: TAPD
entries.body: Daemon software that is the reference implementation of the Taproot Assets protocol, developed by Lightning Labs. `tapd` makes it possible to create (*mint*), send and receive digital assets encoded in Taproot outputs on the Bitcoin blockchain.

entries.title: TAPROOT
entries.body:
A major update to the Bitcoin protocol, adopted through a soft fork in November 2021. This update brings significant improvements in privacy, efficiency and flexibility, by implementing BIP-0340, BIP-0341 and BIP-0342. This update was locked in at block 687,284, on June 12, 2021, when 90% of the blocks generated during a period signaled in favor, thereby showing the miners' readiness to activate the update (*Speedy Trial*). Activation finally took place at block 709,632, on November 14, 2021, almost four years after the first discussions on the subject between Pieter Wuille, Andrew Poelstra and Gregory Maxwell. It was the first attempt at a major update since the thorny activation of SegWit in 2017.

Taproot is also the name of BIP-0341, implemented within the soft fork of the same name, which introduces a new script model called P2TR. A P2TR script locks bitcoins to a single Schnorr public key, called `K`. However, this `K` key is actually an aggregate of a public key `P` and a public key `M`, the latter being calculated from the Merkle root of a list of `scriptPubKey`. Bitcoins locked with a P2TR script can be spent in two distinct ways: either by publishing a signature for the public key `P`, or by satisfying one of the scripts contained in the Merkle tree. The first option is called the “*key path*” and the second the “*script path*”.

entries.title: TAPROOT ASSETS PROTOCOL
entries.body:
A protocol developed by Lightning Labs that makes it possible to issue assets on the main Bitcoin blockchain, taking advantage of the Taproot update. Taproot Assets allows the creation of fungible assets such as stablecoins and non-fungible assets such as NFTs. Taproot Assets can be transferred via regular Bitcoin transactions or via the Lightning Network. This protocol uses *Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Trees* (MS-SMT), a sort of combination of MSTs and SMTs, to ensure the validity and auditability of the assets.

*Taproot Assets Protocol was previously called “TARO.”*

entries.title: TAPROOT CHANNEL
entries.body:
A Lightning channel anchored in a Taproot output (P2TR), rather than in a classic SegWit output (P2WSH). *Taproot channels* take advantage of the improvements brought by the Taproot soft fork activated in November 2021 on Bitcoin.

In the case of a cooperative closure, a *Taproot channel* is more efficient and more private than a traditional SegWit channel: the closing transaction looks like an ordinary Taproot spend via the *key path spend*, indistinguishable from a simple on-chain payment. This property strengthens the privacy of Lightning Network users.

entries.title: TAPSCRIPT
entries.body:
An update whose purpose is to modify certain opcodes of Bitcoin's classic scripting language, in order to define the new scripting language used for P2TR spends via the script path (*script path*). Tapscript was introduced by BIP-0342, implemented with the Taproot soft fork.

In order to implement the various changes associated with Taproot, it proved necessary to revisit the scripting language. That is the purpose of Tapscript, which disables or modifies certain opcodes, and adds new ones.

entries.title: TAPSIGNER
entries.body: An NFC card for signing Bitcoin transactions manufactured by Coinkite. The TapSigner stores a BIP-0032 master private key and makes it possible to sign transactions by bringing the card close to an NFC-compatible phone, via a wallet such as Nunchuk. Having no screen, this card is an affordable signing device, suited to small amounts or to use in multisig.

entries.title: TARO
entries.body: Former name of the Taproot Assets Protocol.

entries.title: TCP
entries.body: Acronym for “*Transmission Control Protocol*.” It is a communication protocol designed to ensure reliable data transmission over the Internet. It establishes a connection, guarantees the order of the data sent, handles retransmission in case of packet loss, and controls congestion.

entries.title: TEN31
entries.body: A venture capital fund specialized in investing in companies of the Bitcoin ecosystem. Founded in 2020, Ten31 takes its name from October 31 (10/31 in the American format), the date the White Paper was published by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008.

entries.title: TERMINAL CONSIGNMENT
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *Terminal Consignment* designates the *transfer consignment* incorporating the final state of a contract, obtained through the *State Transition* generated from the recipient's *Invoice* (*payee*). This mechanism represents the end point of a transfer, gathering all the data necessary to attest that the ownership or the state of the contract has been duly transmitted and validated.

entries.title: TESTNET
entries.body: An alternative version of Bitcoin used exclusively for testing and development purposes. It is a network separate from the main network (*mainnet*), with its own blocks and transactions, allowing developers to test new features, applications and updates without risk to the main network. The testnet also makes it possible to avoid paying transaction fees during tests. The bitcoins used on the testnet have no real value.

entries.title: TESTNET RESET
entries.body:
An operation consisting of relaunching the Bitcoin test network with a new genesis block, thereby erasing the existing history and balances. This mechanism ensures that test coins remain easy to mine and without market value, which is important for the testnet to fulfill its function: to offer a free experimentation environment where developers can test attacks, bugs or new features without financial consequences.

The testnet has been reset three times in Bitcoin's history. The first testnet was introduced in October 2010. A first reset was carried out in February 2011, in order to create what would retrospectively be called “testnet2.” Gavin Andresen then launched “testnet3” in April 2012. After 13 years of service, testnet3 was finally replaced by testnet4 in 2024, defined in BIP-0094, notably because its coins had begun to acquire a market value.

entries.title: TESTNET4
entries.body:
The fourth iteration of Bitcoin's public test network, launched in 2024 to replace testnet3, which had become dysfunctional after 13 years of service. Testnet4 is a network distinct from *mainnet* where the bitcoins (TBTC) have no value, allowing developers to test their applications without financial risk.

Testnet3 suffered from several problems. A bug in the difficulty reset rule (which brought it back to 1 if no block had been found in 20 minutes) regularly caused block storms, pushing the chain height beyond 2.5 million blocks. The block reward had fallen to ~0.014 TBTC, making mining ineffective for distributing test coins. And above all, in 2024, TBTC had begun to be bought and sold for fraudulent airdrops, breaking the fundamental principle of their lack of value.

Testnet4, defined in BIP-0094, fixes the difficulty mechanism by forbidding the 20-minute exception for the first block of each retargeting period and by basing the adjustment calculation on the difficulty of the first block of the previous period rather than on that of the last. It uses port 48333 and a new genesis block. It is supported by Bitcoin Core starting with version 28.0.

entries.title: THE DAO
entries.body: A project launched in 2016 on Ethereum, which aimed to create an autonomous investment fund managed by *smart contracts*. Although mainly linked to Ethereum, The DAO had a significant impact on the evolution of Bitcoin. In June 2016, The DAO fell victim to a massive hack. In response, the Ethereum community carried out a *hard fork*, which turned out to be a resounding failure. This incident consolidated the conservative positions of the *small blockers* during Bitcoin's Blocksize War. They used this event to argue against rapid changes to the Bitcoin protocol, such as those advocated by the *big blockers*, and against the idea of carrying out *hard forks*, as was done on Ethereum following the hack of The DAO.

entries.title: THE EYE OF SATOSHI
entries.body: An open source watchtower implementation for the Lightning Network. A watchtower continuously monitors the Bitcoin blockchain on behalf of a user and automatically intervenes by broadcasting a penalty transaction if a counterparty attempts to cheat by publishing an old channel state.

entries.title: THUNDERHUB
entries.body: An open source web interface for managing and monitoring Lightning Network nodes based on LND. The tool makes it possible to manage payment channels, send and receive on-chain and Lightning payments, rebalance liquidity and consult detailed reports on the node's activity.

entries.title: TIDES
entries.body: Acronym for “*Transparent Index Of Distinct Extended Shares*.” It is a method of calculating miner compensation in the context of mining pools, introduced by the Ocean pool in 2023. This method distributes rewards according to a weighted percentage of the work devoted to the most recently found shares. Each proof is rewarded several times, with a reward calculation that includes transaction fees. This system ensures great precision in miners' payouts, without requiring a custodial intermediary to process payments, unlike other methods such as FPPS. TIDES is designed for transparent compensation.

entries.title: TIME WARP
entries.body:
A theoretical attack on Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism that exploits a flaw in the way block timestamps are verified at the boundary between two retarget periods. Every 2,016 blocks, the protocol recalculates the difficulty target by comparing the timestamp of the first block of the period with that of the last. The attack consists, for a miner who controls a majority of the computing power, of manipulating these timestamps: they set the timestamps of almost all the blocks of the period to the minimum allowed by the *Median Time Past* (MTP) rule, then assign the last block a timestamp in the future, which respects the NAT + 2 hours rule. The protocol then deduces that the period lasted much longer than it actually did, which results in an artificial and unjustified reduction of the difficulty for the following period.

By repeating this process over several successive periods, an attacker could theoretically lower the difficulty until producing blocks at an extreme rate (up to a maximum of 6 blocks per second). This extreme deceleration followed by acceleration would compromise the security of funds protected by *timelocks*, could saturate the bandwidth of the network's nodes, would facilitate certain types of attacks such as eclipse attacks, and would lead to numerous major reorganizations making transaction confirmations unreliable. For the attacker, the main benefit they can derive is to collect the block subsidies much faster than normal.

The “Consensus Cleanup” soft fork proposal (BIP-0054) aims to fix this vulnerability by requiring that the first block of a new difficulty period carry a timestamp that is not more than 2 hours earlier than that of the last block of the previous period. This constraint prevents the extreme manipulation of the time gaps between two retarget periods and therefore prevents this attack.

Note that this attack is made possible by a historical bug (*off-by-one*) introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto in the calculation of the difficulty adjustment. This calculation takes as a basis a duration of 2 weeks (supposed to correspond to `2016 \times 10` minutes), and compares it with the difference between the first and the last block of the period, in order to determine a deviation. The problem is that between the first and the last block of a period, there are in reality only 2015 intervals, and not 2016. For the calculation to be correct, it would have been necessary to compare with the difference between the last block of the previous period and the last block of the current period that has just ended, which would indeed have given 2016 intervals. Besides the fact that this bug very slightly biases the adjustment calculation by about 0.05%, it is above all what makes time warp attacks possible. Indeed, if the comparison were made on the last block of the previous period rather than on the first block of the period that has just ended, there would be an overlap of the periods, which would prevent this type of manipulation. The problem is that to truly fix this historical bug, a hard fork would be needed.

entries.title: TIME-DILATION ATTACK
entries.body:
An attack on the Lightning Network that combines an eclipse attack with a deliberate slowing of block delivery to the victim. The attacker takes control of all the connections of the victim's Bitcoin node, then transmits new blocks to it with a calculated delay (typically just under Bitcoin Core's 30-minute detection threshold). The victim gradually accumulates a lag relative to the real chain. This time offset is exploited to bypass the security mechanisms of the Lightning Network that rely on *timelocks*. For example, the attacker can broadcast an old, revoked commitment transaction on the real network. The victim, whose view of the blockchain is behind, does not detect this attempted fraud in time to publish a penalty transaction before the expiration of the contest delay. The attack requires no mining power.

This concept was formalized in 2020 by Antoine Riard and Gleb Naumenko. Three variants have been identified, the most effective of which (the packet finalization attack) requires only a few hours of eclipse and a single channel with the victim. The countermeasures rely on the use of *watchtowers* on independent infrastructure, the reception of blocks through alternative channels and the strengthening of anti-eclipse protections.

entries.title: TIMELOCK
entries.body:
A smart contract primitive that makes it possible to define a time condition to be met before a transaction can be added to a block. There are two types of timelocks on Bitcoin: 
* The absolute timelock, which specifies a precise moment before which the transaction cannot be included in a block; 
* The relative timelock, which defines a delay starting from the acceptance of a prior transaction. 

The timelock can be defined either as a date expressed in Unix time, or as a block number. Finally, the timelock can apply either to a transaction output through the use of a specific opcode in the locking script (`OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY` or `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY`), or to an entire transaction through the use of the `nLockTime` field, or to a specific input through the use of the `nSequence` field.

*One also sometimes speaks of a “locktime” to refer to a timelock.*

entries.title: TLV
entries.body:
Data encoding format *type-length-value* structured in three fields: a type identifying the nature of the information, a length indicating the size of the data, and a value containing the data itself. This format makes it possible to create extensible messages in which new field types can be added without breaking compatibility with existing implementations.

On the Lightning Network, TLV is used to structure the messages of the BOLT protocol, making it possible to include optional information such as payment metadata or routing data. In the Taproot Assets protocol, each leaf of the asset tree contains a TLV blob that encodes the version, the *asset ID*, the amount held, as well as the signatures and data relating to the asset's previous transfers.

entries.title: TOR
entries.body:
Network of relay servers (*nodes*) that makes it possible to anonymize the origin of TCP connections on the internet. It works by encapsulating data in several layers of encryption. Each relay node removes one layer to reveal the address of the next node, until the final destination is reached. The Tor network ensures anonymity by preventing intermediate nodes from knowing both the origin and the destination of the data, which makes it very difficult for an observer to trace the user's activity. The Tor network can be used with Bitcoin to avoid associating one's IP address with a Bitcoin node, and thus avoid leaking some personal information.

*"Tor" stands for "The Onion Router". It is important to distinguish Tor the network from Tor Browser, a web browser based on Firefox that is specifically designed to use the Tor network.*

entries.title: TPRV
entries.body: Extended private key prefix for Legacy and SegWit V1 accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

entries.title: TPUB
entries.body: Extended public key prefix for Legacy and SegWit V1 accounts on Bitcoin Testnet.

entries.title: TRAMPOLINE ROUTING
entries.body:
Lightning routing method that allows a light node to delegate the construction of the payment path to one or more specialized intermediate nodes called *trampoline nodes*. It is particularly useful for mobile embedded nodes that cannot synchronize the full network graph because of constraints on storage, computing power or intermittent connectivity.

The sender builds a "trampoline onion" that identifies the trampoline nodes by their full identifier. It routes the payment to the first trampoline, which itself computes the route to the next trampoline or to the recipient. The non-trampoline nodes on the route require no update: they relay HTLCs like ordinary payments. To preserve privacy, the sender can chain at least two trampoline nodes, so that none of them knows whether it is routing to the final recipient or to another trampoline. Trampoline nodes charge additional fees for this *pathfinding* service. Trampoline routing can be combined with *blinded paths* to hide the recipient's identity, thus offering complete privacy even from a mobile device.

entries.title: TRANSACTION PINNING
entries.body:
Attack that consists of making the replacement of a transaction prohibitively expensive by exploiting nodes' protections against the waste of bandwidth, CPU and memory. The attacker diverts the rules intended to prevent abuse of the relay system and uses them to block legitimate attempts to increase fees in a multiparty context.

Two main vectors are exploited. The first abuses rule 3 of BIP-0125, which requires that the replacement transaction pay higher absolute fees than the original transaction and all of its children. The attacker attaches a large child transaction with a low fee rate, which forces the victim to pay disproportionately high fees to perform a replacement by RBF. The second vector exploits descendant limits: nodes restrict transactions to 101,000 vbytes of descendants or 25 ancestors/descendants in total. An attacker can saturate these limits with their own child transactions, which completely blocks CPFP.

This attack represents a serious threat to the Lightning Network and other multiparty protocols, where fee management is crucial to meeting settlement time windows. Several countermeasures have been developed: the *CPFP carve-out*, *ephemeral anchors*, v3 transactions and *package relay*.

entries.title: TRANSACTION WITNESS
entries.body:
Refers to a component of Bitcoin transactions that was moved with the SegWit soft fork in order to solve the problem of transaction malleability. The witness contains the signatures and public keys necessary to unlock the bitcoins spent in a transaction. In Legacy transactions, the witness was the sum of the `scriptSig` of all the inputs. In SegWit transactions, the witness is the sum of the `scriptWitness` of each input, and this part of the transaction is now moved into a separate Merkle tree within the block.

Before SegWit, signatures could be slightly modified without being invalidated before a transaction was confirmed, which changed the transaction identifier. This made it difficult to build various protocols, because an unconfirmed transaction could have its identifier changed. By separating the witnesses, SegWit makes transactions non-malleable, because any change in the signatures no longer affects the transaction identifier (TXID), but only the witness identifier (WTXID). In addition to solving the malleability problem, this separation makes it possible to increase the capacity of each block.

entries.title: TRANSITION BUNDLE
entries.body: In the RGB protocol, a *Transition Bundle* refers to a grouping of *State Transitions* belonging to the same contract, all committed simultaneously in a single Bitcoin *witness transaction*. This mechanism makes it possible to consolidate several updates or transfers into a single *on-chain* anchor point, in order to optimize the use of block space.

entries.title: TREZOR
entries.body: Brand of *hardware wallets* made by the Czech company SatoshiLabs, launched in 2014 with the Trezor One, considered the first commercially sold Bitcoin hardware wallet. Trezor offers devices that make it possible to secure private keys offline. The devices run *open source* *firmware*, which allows independent verification of the code by the community. Interaction with the wallet is done through the Trezor Suite application or compatible software such as Sparrow Wallet.

entries.title: TRIMMED HTLC
entries.body:
On the Lightning Network, an HTLC is said to be "*trimmed*" when its value is too low to justify the creation of a dedicated output in the commitment transaction. Concretely, if the HTLC amount is below the channel's *dust limit*, it would be uneconomical to resolve it *on-chain*. Instead of creating a separate output, the value of these HTLCs is absorbed into the transaction fees of the commitment transaction.

This mechanism is essential to allow Lightning channels to relay very small payments, potentially of a single satoshi, without being limited by the dust threshold imposed by the Bitcoin protocol. From an operational standpoint, *trimmed HTLCs* are built and resolved exactly like ordinary HTLCs: they transit normally between nodes and are honored or canceled according to the same rules. The difference only appears if the commitment transaction has to be published *on-chain*, in which case their value is lost to fees instead of being recoverable.

This design nevertheless poses security problems. A malicious actor can create many *trimmed HTLCs* with no intention of resolving them, which forces their counterparty to pay higher transaction fees, or destroys part of the channel's value. Several improvements have been proposed, such as redirecting the value of *trimmed HTLCs* to ephemeral *anchor outputs* or using probabilistic payments.

entries.title: TUMBLEBIT
entries.body: Concept of an anonymous payment hub compatible with Bitcoin proposed in 2016 by Ethan Heilman, Leen AlShenibr, Foteini Baldimtsi, Alessandra Scafuro and Sharon Goldberg. TumbleBit is a bitcoin mixing system that does not require trust in an intermediary. It allows users to make fast, anonymous, off-chain payments via a coordinator called the *Tumbler*. TumbleBit guarantees anonymity by ensuring that even the *Tumbler* cannot link a payer's payment to its recipient. The TumbleBit protocol ensures that the *Tumbler* can neither steal bitcoins nor print fake bitcoins by issuing payments to itself. The anonymity offered by TumbleBit is comparable to that of a Chaum *eCash* system. However, this concept was never widely adopted, as privacy techniques such as the Chaumian coinjoin were preferred to it.

entries.title: TURBO CHANNEL
entries.body:
Lightning channel usable immediately, without waiting for the usual on-chain confirmations. Normally, a Lightning channel is only considered operational after several confirmations of its funding transaction, which generally means several tens of minutes. A *turbo channel*, also called a *zero-conf* channel, removes this wait: both ends of the channel consider it active as soon as the funding transaction is broadcast in the mempools.

This mechanism involves a trust trade-off: as long as the funding transaction is not confirmed, the party that opened the channel could theoretically carry out a double spend by publishing a competing transaction. In practice, this trust is accepted in a setting where the channel opener is a liquidity service provider (LSP) whose reputation would be destroyed by such fraud. Some implementations strengthen security by requiring that the opening transaction come from a multisignature address with a trusted cosigner.

*Turbo channels* are widely used by mobile embedded nodes such as Phoenix, because they allow new users to send and receive payments as soon as the channel is opened, with an experience closer to that of custodial solutions.

entries.title: TWEAK
entries.body:
In the field of cryptography, "tweaking" a public key consists of modifying that key using an additive value called the "tweak" such that it remains usable with knowledge of the original private key and of the tweak. Technically, a tweak is a scalar value that is added to the initial public key. If `P` is the public key and `t` is the tweak, the tweaked public key becomes:
```math
P' = P + tG
```
Where `G` is the generator of the elliptic curve used. This operation makes it possible to obtain a new public key derived from the original key while retaining certain cryptographic properties that allow it to be used. For example, this method is used for Taproot (P2TR) addresses in order to be able to spend either by presenting a Schnorr signature in the traditional way, or by fulfilling one of the conditions set out in a Merkle tree, also called "MAST".

![Tweaked public key combining the key P and the root M of a MAST grouping four Taproot spending conditions A, B, C, D.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/t/tweak/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: TWENTYTWO DEVICES
entries.body: Company founded by Alekos Filini that develops the Portal, a flat-format *hardware wallet* that communicates with *smartphones* exclusively via NFC, with no cable or battery. The Portal's *firmware* is written entirely in Rust and relies on BDK. Both the hardware and the software are fully *open source*.

entries.title: TX - TRANSACTION
entries.body:
In the context of Bitcoin, a transaction (abbreviated "TX") is an operation recorded on the blockchain that transfers ownership of bitcoins from one or more inputs to one or more outputs. Each transaction consumes UTXOs as inputs, which are outputs of previous transactions, and creates new UTXOs as outputs, which can be used as inputs in future transactions.

Each input includes a reference to an existing output as well as a signature script (`scriptSig`) that fulfills the spending conditions (`scriptPubKey`) established by the output it refers to. This is what makes it possible to unlock bitcoins. Outputs define new spending conditions (`scriptPubKey`) for the transferred bitcoins, often in the form of a public key or an address with which the bitcoins are now associated.

entries.title: TX0
entries.body:
Preparatory transaction specific to the Whirlpool protocol, which constitutes the first step before the coinjoin cycles. The Tx0 takes one or more UTXOs from the user's wallet and restructures them into several outputs calibrated to match exactly the amounts of the chosen coinjoin pool, in addition to the mining fees for the first cycle.

Concretely, the Tx0 produces several types of outputs: UTXOs of a fixed amount intended to enter the coinjoin cycles (which will go into the premix account), an output for the coordinator's fees, and possibly a change output (the "*doxxic change*") which corresponds to the excess that cannot be integrated into the pool.

entries.title: TXID - TRANSACTION IDENTIFIER
entries.body: Unique identifier associated with each Bitcoin transaction. It is generated by calculating the `SHA256d` hash of the transaction data. The TXID serves as a reference to find a specific transaction within the blockchain. It is also used to refer to a UTXO, via an *outpoint* which is essentially the concatenation of the TXID of a previous transaction and the index of the designated output (also called "*vout*"). For post-SegWit transactions, the TXID no longer takes the transaction's witness into account, which makes it possible to eliminate malleability.

entries.title: UNCONFIRMED TRANSACTION
entries.body: Bitcoin transaction that has been broadcast on the network, but has not yet been included in a block by a miner. It remains in the nodes' mempools, waiting to get confirmations. Confirmation occurs when the transaction is included in a valid block added to the blockchain. The time needed for a transaction to be confirmed depends on the transaction fees paid and on system congestion.
